sections.title: SOV Word Order
sections.rule: Hindi sentences follow Subject + Object + Verb order — the verb almost always comes last. Modifiers, time and place words sit before the verb, and the sentence closes with the conjugated verb plus its auxiliary.
sections.example_ref: English: I learn Hindi. / She reads a book.
sections.note: Romanized: main hindī sīkhtā hūn / vah kitāb paṛhtī hai. Whatever else you add, put the verb at the very end.

sections.title: Grammatical Gender of Nouns
sections.rule: Every Hindi noun is either masculine or feminine, and adjectives and verbs agree with it. Many masculine nouns end in -आ and many feminine in -ई, but gender must be learned per word.
sections.example_ref: English: a good boy / a good girl.
sections.note: Romanized: acchā laṛkā / acchī laṛkī. The adjective अच्छा changes to अच्छी for the feminine noun.

sections.title: Verb Agreement with Gender
sections.rule: In the present and future, the verb takes -ता for masculine, -ती for feminine and -ते for masculine plural / respectful. The verb agrees with the subject's gender and number.
sections.example_ref: English: He goes. / She goes.
sections.note: Romanized: vah jātā hai / vah jātī hai. Same pronoun वह, but the verb ending signals he vs she.

sections.title: Present Habitual Tense
sections.rule: Form the habitual present with verb-stem + ता/ती/ते plus the auxiliary हूँ/है/हो/हैं matching the subject. It covers habitual and general-truth actions ('I eat', 'they go').
sections.example_ref: English: I drink tea every day. / They go to school.
sections.note: Romanized: main roz cāy pītā hūn / ve skūl jāte hain. Auxiliary: हूँ (I), है (he/she/it), हो (tum), हैं (we/they/āp).

sections.title: Past Tense with था/थी/थे
sections.rule: For the habitual/continuous past, use the -ता/ती/ते form followed by था/थी/थे ('used to'). था/थी/थे is also the past of होना (to be) and agrees in gender and number.
sections.example_ref: English: I used to live in the village. / They were very happy.
sections.note: Romanized: main gānv men rahtā thā / ve bahut khuś the. था=m.sg, थी=f, थे=m.pl/respect, थीं=f.pl.

sections.title: Postpositions, Not Prepositions
sections.rule: Hindi marks relationships with postpositions that come AFTER the noun, not before it. Common ones are में (in), पर (on), से (from/with), को (to), का/के/की (of).
sections.example_ref: English: The book is on the table. / I have come from Delhi.
sections.note: Romanized: kitāb mez par hai / main dillī se āyā hūn. English 'on the table' → Hindi 'table on' (मेज़ पर).

sections.title: The Postposition को (ko)
sections.rule: को marks the indirect object ('to/for') and specific/animate direct objects. With verbs of liking or needing, the experiencer takes को/मुझे, so the sentence is literally 'to-me X is pleasing'.
sections.example_ref: English: I like Hindi. / I gave the book to Ram.
sections.note: Romanized: mujhe hindī pasand hai / mainne rām ko kitāb dī. मुझे = मुझ + को (to me); तुझे, उसे, हमें work the same way.

sections.title: Obligation & Ability Verbs
sections.rule: Use the infinitive (-ना form) with चाहिए (should/need), सकना (can), or पड़ना (have to) to express need, ability and compulsion. The experiencer usually takes को/मुझे.
sections.example_ref: English: I have to go now. / He can speak Hindi.
sections.note: Romanized: mujhe abhī jānā hai / vah hindī bol saktā hai. सकना attaches to the bare stem (बोल), not the full infinitive.

sections.title: Future Tense
sections.rule: Form the future from the stem + ऊँगा/एगा/एँगे etc., agreeing in person, gender and number. The -गा/गी/गे ending is essentially 'will' fused onto the subjunctive.
sections.example_ref: English: I will go to Delhi tomorrow. / She will do this work.
sections.note: Romanized: main kal dillī jāūngā / vah yah kām karegī. Endings carry gender: जाऊँगा (m.) vs जाऊँगी (f.).

sections.title: The Ergative ने Construction
sections.rule: With transitive verbs in the perfective past, the subject takes the postposition ने and the verb agrees with the OBJECT, not the subject. Intransitive verbs never take ने.
sections.example_ref: English: I read the book. / The boy ate the mangoes.
sections.note: Romanized: mainne kitāb paṛhī / laṛke ne ām khāe. पढ़ी is feminine because किताब is feminine — the verb ignores 'I'.

sections.title: The Oblique Case
sections.rule: Before a postposition, nouns and adjectives shift to the oblique case. Masculine -आ nouns become -ए (लड़का→लड़के), and all plurals take -ओं (लड़कों). Feminine nouns usually stay the same in the singular.
sections.example_ref: English: Call the boy. / There are three chairs in the room.
sections.note: Romanized: laṛke ko bulāo / kamre men tīn kursiyān hain. लड़का→लड़के and कमरा→कमरे only because a postposition (को, में) follows.

sections.title: Continuous & Perfect Aspects
sections.rule: For the progressive, use stem + रहा/रही/रहे + auxiliary ('am doing'). For a completed action, use stem + चुका/चुकी/चुके ('have already done'). Both agree in gender and number.
sections.example_ref: English: I am eating food. / She has already gone.
sections.note: Romanized: main khānā khā rahā hūn / vah jā cukī hai. रहा marks ongoing action; चुका stresses that it is finished.

sections.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
sections.rule: Compare with X से (than X) plus the adjective, optionally with ज़्यादा (more) or कम (less). For the superlative, use सबसे ('than all') before the adjective.
sections.example_target_2: वह कक्षा में सबसे अच्छा है।
sections.example_ref: English: This is bigger than that. / He is the best in the class.
sections.note: Romanized: yah usse baṛā hai / vah kakṣā men sabse acchā hai. The adjective itself does not change form; से does the comparing.

sections.title: Respect Levels: आप, तुम, तू
sections.rule: Hindi has three 'you' levels: आप (formal/respectful, plural verb), तुम (familiar, -ते हो / -ओ endings), and तू (intimate or rude, singular). Choosing the pronoun signals the social relationship.
sections.example_ref: English: Where are you going? (formal) / Where are you going? (familiar)
sections.note: Romanized: āp kahān jāte hain / tum kahān jāte ho. Use आप with elders and strangers; तू can offend unless used with intimates.

sections.title: Imperatives & Polite Requests
sections.rule: Command forms match the 'you' level: तू + bare stem (बैठ), तुम + ओ (बैठो), आप + इए (बैठिए, please sit). Negate a command with मत before the verb.
sections.example_ref: English: Please sit here. / Don't go right now.
sections.note: Romanized: kṛpayā yahān baiṭhie / abhī mat jāo. मत is for commands; नहीं negates statements.

sections.title: Conjunctive Participle कर/के
sections.rule: To link two actions by the same subject ('having done X, then Y'), add कर (or के) to the first verb's stem. Only the final verb is fully conjugated for tense.
sections.example_ref: English: Having eaten, he fell asleep. / Go home and rest.
sections.note: Romanized: khānā khākar vah so gayā / ghar jākar ārām karo. करना becomes करके, not खाकर — कर itself uses के.

sections.title: Conditional अगर...तो
sections.rule: Real conditionals use अगर (if) in the first clause and तो (then) in the second. For hypothetical/unreal conditions, use अगर...होता...तो...होता with the -ता counterfactual form.
sections.example_target: अगर बारिश हुई तो मैं नहीं आऊँगा।
sections.example_target_2: अगर तुम पढ़ते तो पास हो जाते।
sections.example_ref: English: If it rains, I won't come. / If you had studied, you would have passed.
sections.note: Romanized: agar bāriś huī to main nahīn āūngā / agar tum paṛhte to pās ho jāte. अगर can be dropped, but तो usually stays.

sections.title: Subjunctive for Wish & Doubt
sections.rule: The subjunctive (stem + ऊँ/ए/एँ, no -गा) expresses wishes, possibility, doubt, and 'shall I?' questions. It often follows शायद (maybe), चाहता हूँ कि, or ताकि (so that).
sections.example_ref: English: Maybe he will come tomorrow. / Shall I come in?
sections.note: Romanized: śāyad vah kal āe / kyā main andar āūn? Drop the -गा of the future and you have the subjunctive.

sections.title: Compound Verbs (लेना/देना/जाना)
sections.rule: A main verb stem plus a 'light' verb (लेना, देना, जाना, डालना) adds nuance — completion, direction, or benefit — without changing the core meaning. The light verb carries the tense.
sections.example_ref: English: He read the whole book (through). / He suddenly fell asleep.
sections.note: Romanized: usne pūrī kitāb paṛh lī / vah acānak so gayā. लेना = action for oneself; देना = for others; जाना = change of state.

sections.title: Passive Voice
sections.rule: Form the passive with the perfective participle + जाना conjugated for tense. The agent, if named, takes के द्वारा or से. It is common for rules, notices and impersonal statements.
sections.example_ref: English: Hindi is spoken here. / The door was opened.
sections.note: Romanized: yahān hindī bolī jātī hai / darvāzā kholā gayā. The participle agrees with the subject: बोली (f.) with हिंदी.

sections.title: Relative–Correlative जो...वह
sections.rule: Instead of embedding a clause, Hindi pairs a relative word (जो, जहाँ, जब, जितना) with a correlative (वह, वहाँ, तब, उतना). The जो-clause usually comes first.
sections.example_target: जो मेहनत करता है, वह सफल होता है।
sections.example_target_2: जहाँ चाह है, वहाँ राह है।
sections.example_ref: English: One who works hard succeeds. / Where there is a will, there is a way.
sections.note: Romanized: jo mehnat kartā hai, vah saphal hotā hai / jahān cāh hai, vahān rāh hai. Think 'which... that...' as a matched pair.

sections.title: Causative Verbs
sections.rule: Hindi builds causatives in layers: base verb → first causative (-आना, do it) → second causative (-वाना, have it done by someone). This lets you say who actually causes the action.
sections.example_target: माँ ने बच्चे को खाना खिलाया।
sections.example_ref: English: The mother fed the child. / I got my hair cut.
sections.note: Romanized: mān ne bacce ko khānā khilāyā / mainne bāl kaṭvāe. खाना (eat) → खिलाना (feed) → खिलवाना (have someone fed).
